text:
Marco: Quick follow-up on the control-plane separation RFC — I sketched ownership and cutover tradeoffs for per-customer VPC peering attachments. Two high-level paths: (A) Redwood manages attachments (cross-account role + managed routes), (B) Customer owns attachments and we supply route manifests. Want to align on who takes ownership and how to avoid route-table churn during cutover. :thinking:
Amy: This is great. My top concern is route table scaling and propagation noise. With option A we can centralize logic but we need strong rate-limits and backoff to avoid AWS route propagation storms. Also we must handle large customers who already hit RT limits.
Jin: Agree. One pattern that helps is using a regional managed prefix-list we update per-tenant, then reference the prefix-list from the customer's route tables instead of pushing N individual routes. That keeps entries small and makes cutovers atomic. Downsides: prefix-lists are limited to 1000 entries in some regions, and it adds an indirection layer.
Marco: Exact. For clarity, example terraform we'd use for option A (managed attachment in customer account via cross-account role):
```
resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "cp_peer" {
  provider = aws.assume_redwood[account_id]
  vpc_id   = var.redwood_vpc_id
  peer_vpc_id = var.customer_vpc_id
  auto_accept = false
}
# then accept using a customer-side role or API call once created
```
Marco: For option B we'd emit a manifest (YAML) the customer applies; we validate with a preflight checker and request a webhook when routes are ready. This is safer ops-wise but slower for onboarding and puts burden on customers.
Amy: Another operational concern: certificate and control-plane endpoint lifecycle. If Redwood owns attachment lifecycle, we can gate cert rollover behind a phased route swap to avoid transient 403s. If customers own attachments, cert rollover needs a coordination API.
Jin: Also watch for route flaps: during cutover we should disable route propagation, apply new static routes, then reconverge. We should provide a phased checklist for SRE-run cutovers (dry-run, dry-route-announce, failover window, rollback).
Sam: +1 on phased checklist. For large customers (>500 routes) we should recommend Dedicated transit model (TGW or Partner Transit) instead of per-customer peering. That offloads route limits and reduces per-tenant operator work.
deploy-bot: Scheduling note: @Marco requested a short spike to prototype prefix-list approach. Job created: spike/prefixlist-prototype, ETA 3d.
Amy: Questions for the spike: how quickly can we update a managed prefix-list across 3 regions? What's worst-case propagation window? Please record numbers. Also include failure modes: partial apply, rate-limited API errors, IAM cross-account permission denials.
Marco: Proposal: default to option A (Redwood-managed attachments) for self-serve customers up to 250 route-equivalents; fallback guidance to transit pattern for bigger customers. We'll add a lock-step cutover playbook (dry-run -> staged route replace -> monitor BGP/health -> finalize) and a small control-plane API for cert rollover signals. If no objections I'll write an RFC addendum and include the spike results. :+1:
Jin: Sounds good. Add metrics to the playbook: route propagation time, number of route API errors, percent of cutovers requiring rollback.
Amy: Also surface a customer-facing checklist so self-serve customers know expected downtime windows and required IAM role.
Marco: Thanks — I'll take the follow-ups: write spike ticket (linked), draft RFC addendum, and a cutover playbook doc. Will ping when drafts are ready.
Sam: Nice. If you want ops support for cutovers ping SRE and include runbook steps.
Marco: Done — thanks everyone.
